name: Pediatric medial approach to the distal humerus
corridor: Medial supracondylar exposure with direct identification and protection of the ulnar nerve

positioning.text: Position supine with arm supported, medial elbow accessible, and fluoroscopy able to obtain orthogonal views without stressing fixation.

setup.text: Document ulnar-nerve function, plan fragment and flexor-pronator management, and decide whether only a mini-open pin window or full exposure is required.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark medial supracondylar ridge, medial epicondyle, olecranon, ulnar groove, and flexor-pronator mass.

incision.text: Center a 2-3 cm extensile incision across medial epicondyle; for pin visualization alone, use a roughly 1.5 cm incision with blunt subcutaneous dissection.

superficial_interval.text: Identify and protect the posterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, then locate the ulnar nerve proximally, in its groove, and between FCU heads.

deep_interval.text: Retract the protected ulnar nerve gently, release medial intermuscular septum proximally as needed, and retract flexor-pronator mass anteriorly for capsular access.

layers.text: Skin, cutaneous-nerve plane, ulnar-nerve plane, medial septum/flexor-pronator origin, capsule, then medial distal humerus.

structures_encountered.text: Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, ulnar nerve, FCU heads, medial septum, flexor-pronator origin, capsule, and medial epicondyle are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Ulnar nerve and its FCU motor branch, medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, physis, and medial collateral ligament are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Preserve the first FCU motor branch if transposition is necessary and never place a medial pin without knowing the ulnar-nerve position.

retraction_hazards.text: Use a broad smooth retractor or soft loop without sustained ulnar-nerve traction; avoid focal pressure behind medial epicondyle.

exposure.text: Exposes medial epicondyle for reduction and fixation, permits ulnar-nerve exploration, and provides direct protection during medial pin insertion.

limitations.text: Opening the joint medially is not an ideal primary exposure for routine pediatric supracondylar fracture reduction.

extensions.text: Release medial septum approximately 3 cm proximally or open capsule longitudinally only when the pathology requires broader medial access.

indications.text: Use for medial epicondyle fixation, ulnar-nerve exploration, and mini-open protection during crossed K-wire fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid routine extensile medial arthrotomy for a reducible supracondylar fracture without medial pathology or nerve concern.

implant_implications.text: Place screws or wires under direct ulnar-nerve protection and verify that implants do not tether nerve, violate joint, or injure the physis.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use AP, lateral, and oblique images to confirm reduction and that medial pins or screws remain extra-articular with safe trajectories.

closure.text: Repair capsule when opened, restore flexor-pronator tissues, confirm a tension-free ulnar nerve, and close with fine absorbable sutures.

complications.text: Complications include ulnar neuropathy, sensory neuroma, stiffness, nonunion, valgus instability, growth disturbance, infection, and symptomatic hardware.

bailouts.text: If reduction is blocked by incarcerated fragment or nerve, enlarge under direct visualization rather than force percutaneous fixation.

procedure_applications.condition: A medial epicondyle fracture requires open reduction or direct ulnar-nerve assessment
A mini-open exposure is chosen for safe medial crossed-pin placement

questions.question: Which cutaneous nerve commonly crosses the incision?
questions.answer: The posterior branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve.

questions.question: What does a mini-open medial incision accomplish?
questions.answer: Direct visualization and protection of the ulnar nerve during medial pin placement.

questions.question: Which motor branch must be preserved?
